title: Three kinds of word: noun, verb, adjective
summary: Almost every Japanese word is a noun, a verb or an い-adjective, and the special kinds of noun each have just one extra power.

blocks.text: Textbooks pour Japanese words into English boxes (adverb, adjective, preposition) and the confusion never ends. The course makes it much simpler: nearly every word is a **noun**, a **verb** or an **adjective**. Besides those there are the **particles**, which are the nuts and bolts, and a handful of real connecting words such as けど.
Verbs and adjectives are easy to spot

A verb always ends in an **う-row kana** (う, く, す, る, ...). An adjective always ends in the kana **い**. Both must show that ending in kana, never inside a kanji. These last kana are the part that changes: 食べる becomes 食べた, 高い becomes 高かった.
So if a word has none of those endings, it is a **noun**. A word written only in kanji is a noun about 99 times out of 100. Japanese is a very **noun-centered** language.
Some nouns have exactly one power that ordinary nouns lack. Each group is still a noun. Everything else about it is plain noun behavior.
These three groups are the textbook's な-adjectives, する verbs and adverbs. In this course they are all just nouns with one extra power.
An adjectival noun may use the soft copula **な** to hang in front of another noun.

blocks.jp: 静かな部屋で勉強する。

blocks.text: Any ordinary noun that fits the meaning can work as an adverb if you add **に**, as in 静かに歩く ("walk quietly"). An adverbial noun like ゆっくり simply may leave the に out. The first needs it, the second does not.

blocks.jp: 電車がゆっくり止まった。

blocks.text: A する noun may drop を and fuse with する. Both of these are the same sentence. Without する, a word like 勉強 is still just a noun, which is why 勉強が好きだ works with no verb in sight.

blocks.jp: 毎日、日本語の勉強をする。
blocks.en: I study Japanese every day. (with を)

blocks.jp: 毎日、日本語を勉強する。
blocks.en: I study Japanese every day. (を dropped, the noun fused with する)
(I) like study. (the noun, no する needed)

blocks.text: Watch out for あまり and ずいぶん

**あまり** is a noun meaning "excess" and **ずいぶん** is a noun meaning "a fair amount". Japanese often says less than it means (understatement). English does this too: "It doesn't look too good" really means "it looks bad", and "you're pretty good" means "you're very good".

blocks.jp: ご飯のあまりを食べた。
blocks.en: I ate the leftover rice. (あまり as a plain noun)

blocks.jp: 悲しみのあまり泣いた。
blocks.en: I cried from an excess of sadness.
I do not study much. (literally: I do not study an excess)
You're pretty good, aren't you! (really: very good)

items: Nearly every word is a **noun**, **verb** or **adjective**.
Verbs end in an **う-row kana**; adjectives end in **い**; anything else is a noun.
Adjectival nouns, する nouns and adverbial nouns are still nouns, each with one extra power.
Words that dictionaries call adverbs are nearly always nouns used without に.
